analysis: The sustainable-technology plan combines physical science, mathematical and statistical tools, product design and business. Sustainability Essentials II teaches material structure, crystallography, stress and strain and sustainable materials. R3 examines materials separation, recovery and recycling techniques, and its practical work supports a bounded laboratory contribution. Renewable System Design adds technical and economic energy analysis. Building with Nature applies ecological processes to water and coastal design. Consumer Product Design includes working mechanisms, prototyping, material choices, costs and production scaling. Life Cycle Analysis and the regional partner research project address sustainability inquiry, with project content dependent on the partner brief. The computational plan adds numerical methods, linear systems and signal work, robotic motion, machine learning, algorithms and optimisation, and AI decision-making under uncertainty. AI Ethics and the newly selected Business & Economy in the Age of AI link adoption, regulation, fairness and productivity to business decisions. The substitution retains Consumer Product Design and Market Research as applied projects while keeping the computational direction coherent. The shared business courses give finance, market evidence, entrepreneurship and strategy. Description-only courses contribute within their documented scope: Advanced Calculus gives multivariable work, Renewable System Design gives applied system assessment, Strategy & Digital Transformation gives planning and industry cases, and Market Research gives actual research and analysis. The two plans each have nine unique courses. Neither reproduces Maastricht’s integrated materials, industrial processes, lab sequence or mandatory thesis internship. A lab-led alternative lacks sustained engineering lab content, and a leadership-led alternative would dilute the engineering focus.
